Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Vignette:
John, a 30-year-old African-American man who works as a curriculum designer, had been struggling with his past for several months. The traumatic event that continues to haunt him was a period of severe physical abuse by his former romantic partner. This deeply painful experience left lasting marks on both his body and psyche. The night John remembers most vividly was one where the smell of alcohol permeated their apartment. His ex-partner had come home drunk, and the sharp acrid smell of burnt food from an overheated pan filled the kitchen. As he recalls this moment now, it's as if time has paused and the terror returns in full force. He can still feel the pain coursing through his body, the same parts that were bruised and broken during those attacks. John had come to believe that the person he once was is no longer recognizable to him. The man who faced his ex-partner with hope for a better future has been replaced by someone who constantly monitors their environment for potential threats. He feels deeply contaminated by what happened, as if there’s an indelible mark on his being that can never be erased. The triggers are numerous and often unavoidable. Conversations about family life at work send waves of unease through him, particularly when colleagues casually mention their loving families or how they support each other. These comments remind John not only of the abuse he endured but also of the lack of familial support during those difficult times. He tries to avoid such conversations as much as possible, sometimes even excusing himself from meetings that might touch on these topics. John’s daily life has become a series of small evasions and precautions. When walking home from work or out in public spaces, he is acutely aware of any scent reminiscent of alcohol or burnt food. Even the faintest whiff can bring back intense memories of that night, causing his heart to race and his hands to tremble. At times, when these triggers are particularly strong, John experiences a physical pain in the same areas where he was hurt during the abuse. The terror returns as vividly as it did then, leaving him feeling trapped by his own thoughts and sensations. These memories are not just abstract; they feel like real-time events replaying inside his mind. The injustice of what happened to John has become a pervasive theme in how he views the world. He feels that nothing has been done about his situation despite knowing that such abuse is deeply unfair. This sense of powerlessness and unresolved anger sometimes manifests as irritability at work, which has led to strained relationships with some colleagues. John had tried to carry on as normally as possible, but the accumulation of these triggers and memories began to take a toll. He found himself missing deadlines and becoming increasingly isolated from his coworkers. His performance reviews reflected this decline, and he was warned that further lapses could jeopardize his job security. What finally brought John to seek help was an incident at work where he had a panic attack during a presentation due to the accidental mention of family dynamics by one of his colleagues. The room went silent as he struggled to regain composure, but it only made things worse. After that day, John realized that continuing down this path would not lead to any meaningful recovery. In therapy, John hopes to address these triggers and memories in a safe space where he can begin to understand them without reliving the terror. He is most afraid of being forever trapped by his past but also holds onto hope for reclaiming parts of himself that feel lost. Through treatment, John aims to regain a sense of control over his life and find peace with his experiences.
